samples.summary: Revision-preview depth cap counts only `row` nodes, so deep non-row tree nesting still recurses unbounded
samples.evidence: `normalizeYsonTreeNode` only increments `depth` when `node.type === 'row'` and only refuses to descend when `isRow && depth >= MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH` (line 159-165). The walk otherwise recurses over `node.children` for *every* node type. A Yorkie `Tree` has no server-side schema, so any collaborator who can push to the document can write e.g. `cell > cell > cell > …` or `block > block > …` tens of thousands deep with ordinary Tree edits; `unwrapYsonScalars` returns `Tree`-tagged subtrees by reference (unwrap-yson.ts:98) so it does not touch them, leaving this walk as the first and only structural traversal. Attacker: a workspace member with write access poisons a doc, then any user opening that revision in the history panel gets `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` out of `parseDocsSnapshot` (revision-preview.tsx:88) instead of a preview. The file's own comment concedes the bound rests on `YSON.parse` giving out first — i.e. on SDK internals, not on this guard. Impact is a client-side preview crash (surfaced as a role="alert"), which is why this is minor rather than higher.
searchedFor: checked docsTreeToDocument/treeNodeToBlock recursion shape in packages/docs/src/model/crdt-tree.ts

samples.summary: `Math.max(...rows.map(...))` spreads over peer-controlled row/cell counts remain on other untrusted-input paths the diff did not fix
samples.evidence: This diff fixes exactly this hazard in two places (`range-slices.ts:57` and `selection.ts:199`, both citing "`Math.max(...rows)` throws `RangeError` past ~100k arguments, and the row count is a peer's to choose"), but leaves the identical pattern in place where the same untrusted data flows: `serialize/markdown.ts:180` spreads one argument per table row of a peer-written `tableData` (reached by copy-as-markdown and markdown export), and `view/clipboard.ts:323`, `:865`, `:945`, `:1029` spread one argument per row of a pasted payload/HTML — clipboard content an attacker page can set before the user pastes. Attacker: write (or have the victim copy) a table with ~150k rows; the spread throws `RangeError: too many function arguments` out of the export/paste handler, aborting the operation. Same class, same input provenance, unfixed — so the hardening reads as complete when it is not.
searchedFor: read the two fixed sites in selection.ts and range-slices.ts

samples.summary: The merge-expansion budget is opt-in; the toolbar read path still runs the superlinear expansion unbounded over a peer-sized table
samples.evidence: `expandCellRangeForMerges` defaults `budgetCells = Infinity` and only `normalizeCellRange` (selection.ts:214) passes `MAX_MERGE_EXPANSION_CELLS`. The doc comment justifies this by saying the other callers are "one local gesture over one table, not once per peer per paint" — but `computeTableMergeContext` (table-merge-context.ts:53) is reached from `getTableMergeContext` (editor.ts:4392), a read-path accessor the toolbar/menu queries to compute enable-state, not a one-shot write. Its `tableData` comes from `doc.getBlock(tableBlockId)`, i.e. a table whose row/column count a remote peer chose (rows are structure, so none of the numeric bands reach them), and the expansion is a fixed-point `while (changed)` loop whose covered cells each backtrack over the area above-left of them. A peer who writes a large table full of orphan covered cells (`colSpan: 0` with no owner) makes any local cell selection in it hang the tab through this unbudgeted call, which is the very hazard the budget was introduced for. The trade-off (exactness for write paths) is sound; the gap is that this particular caller is a render/read path, not a write.

samples.summary: `MAX_MERGE_EXPANSION_CELLS` (262,144) bounds the call but is large enough to still degrade the render path under several peers
samples.evidence: `const MAX_MERGE_EXPANSION_CELLS = 1 << 18;` is charged per `normalizeCellRange` call, and `computeSelectionRects` normalizes once per peer selection per paint (selection.ts:688). With a hostile table shaped to spend the whole budget, each peer selection costs ~262k cell reads per frame; a handful of peers (or a few presence updates per second) puts the render loop into the millions of reads per frame. The guard turns an infinite hang into a bounded one, which is the right direction, but the constant is generous enough that the peer-driven jank/DoS is not fully closed. Hardening suggestion only.
searchedFor: traced computeSelectionRects callers for peer selections

samples.summary: A single writer can permanently poison a document into an uncopyable state (availability, by design)
samples.evidence: `documentHasTableAtNestingCap(content)` makes `copyContent` throw `BadRequestException` for any doc whose tree holds a table at depth >= 32. Because the readers truncate rather than repair, a collaborator who writes such a table through the raw Yorkie SDK (the frontend/API producers all cap, but a direct SDK peer does not) leaves the document permanently uncopyable — 'Make a copy' and the template-gallery 'use this template' path both fail from then on, and `writeFullDocument`/`writeDocsRoot` likewise refuse every whole-document rewrite (header/footer edits). Refusing beats replicating a deletion, so this is the right call, but it is worth noting that the new failure mode is permanent and reachable by anyone with write access, with no repair path in-product. Reported for visibility; this needs write access, which already permits content destruction, hence nit.
searchedFor: checked packages/backend/src/yorkie/yorkie-auth-enforcement.ts existence for peer write gating

finding.summary: New nesting cap is silently disabled on three write paths: `buildRowNode`/`buildCellNode` are called without the now-required `depth`, so `depth` becomes `undefined` → `NaN` and `depth >= MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH` is never true
finding.evidence: This delta changed the signatures to `buildCellNode(cell: TableCell, depth: number)` (line 417) and `buildRowNode(row: TableRow, depth: number)` (line 425), but three existing call sites were not updated: `insertTableRow` → `buildRowNode(row)` (line 2775), `insertTableColumn` → `buildCellNode(cells[r])` (line 2818), `updateTableCell` → `buildCellNode(cell)` (line 2858). These are TS2554 arity errors, and packages/frontend runs no `tsc` (package.json has only `vite build`, `eslint`, `vitest`), so they ship. At runtime the chain is: `buildCellNode(c, undefined)` → `buildBlockNode(b, undefined)` → `undefined >= 32` is false → `buildRowNode(row, undefined + 1)` = `NaN` → `NaN >= 32` is false and `NaN + 1` stays `NaN` forever. Every nested table written through a cell update, a row insert or a column insert is therefore written uncapped — the exact producer-side guard the diff's own comment says makes the readers/serializers safe ("Without the cap a model that never came out of this CRDT — a DOCX import, a paste — could write a chain deeper than every reader's stack"). `updateTableCell` is the workhorse path for cell content (including pasted cells holding nested tables), so the guard is bypassed on the most-used path while reading as covered. The only new test (`tests/app/docs/yorkie-doc-store.test.ts:3650-3670`) exercises `setDocument`/`writeFullDocument`, so CI stays green.

verdict.reason: The finding claims three call sites invoke `buildRowNode`/`buildCellNode` without the required `depth`, producing NaN and disabling the nesting cap. The code does not read that way. All three paths compute the depth first via `resolveTableRowDepth` and pass it: `insertTableRow` does `const { path: tablePath, rowDepth } = this.resolveTableRowDepth(tableBlockId); const rowNode = buildRowNode(row, rowDepth);` (yorkie-doc-store.ts:2844-2845); `insertTableColumn` does `buildCellNode(cells[r], rowDepth)` (:2877, :2888); `updateTableCell` does `buildCellNode(cell, rowDepth)` (:2927-2928). `resolveTableRowDepth` (:2785-2794) returns `blockPathNestingDepth(path, region) + 1`, matching the `depth + 1` rows convention in `buildBlockNode` (:400), and `blockPathNestingDepth` (:1663-1669) returns a finite number. So no `undefined`/`NaN` enters the chain and the `depth >= MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH` cap at :398 is active on these paths. A repo-wide grep finds no zero-arg call sites in source at all — the only ones are in an archived planning markdown (docs/tasks/archive/2026/03/20260329-table-granular-updates-todo.md:251,285,326), which is not executed. The specific lines cited by the finding (2775, 2818, 2858) contain unrelated code. Premise absent, so the alleged bypass cannot occur.

finding.summary: Incremental block writes restart the depth counter at 0 regardless of how deep in the tree the node is inserted, so the nesting cap only binds on full-document writes
finding.evidence: `buildBlockNode(block)` is called with the default `depth = 0` at lines 1723 (replace block), 2312 and 2335 (insert block), 2371 (insert blocks), 2505 and 2584 — all of which can target a path inside an arbitrarily deep table cell (`resolveBlockTreePath` builds `[...tablePath, rowIdx, cellIdx, blockIdx]` recursively, line 1124). A table block inserted into a cell that already sits at depth 31 is serialized as if it were at depth 0, so up to 32 further levels are written into the CRDT past the cap. Nothing gates the gesture either: `Doc.insertTableInCell` (packages/docs/src/model/document.ts:885) and its caller `editor.ts:4237` perform no depth check, so a user (or a script driving the editor API) can nest tables one level at a time indefinitely. The resulting CRDT holds rows every reader truncates, and — because of the refusal added in this delta — every subsequent `writeFullDocument` on that document then throws. The cap is therefore enforced only on the one path (`writeFullDocument`) that also refuses outright, and not on the paths that actually grow nesting.

verdict.reason: The finding's central presence claim — that incremental block writers call `buildBlockNode(block)` with a default/zeroed `depth`, leaving the nesting cap enforced only in `writeFullDocument` — is not true of this repository. `buildBlockNode` at packages/frontend/src/app/docs/yorkie-doc-store.ts:386 declares `depth: number` with NO default, and a helper `blockPathNestingDepth` (1663-1669) derives the depth from the tree path's `[row, cell, block]` triplet count. Every incremental writer passes it: `updateBlock` (1756), `insertBlockAfter` (2376), `insertBlocksAfter` (2415-2416), `splitBlock` (2499 computing `blockDepth`, consumed at 2560 and 2646), and the table row/cell writers via `resolveTableRowDepth` (2785-2794 -> 2845, 2888, 2928). The only `depth = 0` call sites are structurally top-level: header/footer region replacement (975, 1016), the body top-level `insertBlock` whose path is `[index + off]` (2347), and `writeFullDocument` (3352, 3355, 3360) — all of which are at nesting depth 0 by construction. The specific lines cited as evidence contain other code entirely: 1723 is a JSDoc comment for `setBlockByRegion`, 2312-2319 is the inline `styleByPath` loop, 2335 is the `insertBlock` signature, 2371 is a comment asserting the depth IS inherited, 2505 is `movesHeadingMemory`, 2584 is an inline-text push inside `splitBlock`. Since the cap is in fact applied on the paths the finding says it is absent from, the described weakness does not exist here.
